title: Can ordinary people do great evil?
teaches: Arendt at the Eichmann trial and the banality of evil

parts.title: The man in the glass booth

blocks.text: In May 1960, Israeli agents seized a man on a quiet street in a suburb of Buenos Aires, where he had lived for ten years as Ricardo Klement, a worker at a car factory. He was Adolf Eichmann, the SS officer who had organised the transport of millions of Jews from across Europe to the ghettos and death camps of the Holocaust. He was flown secretly to Israel. His trial opened in Jerusalem in April 1961, and he sat through it in a booth of bulletproof glass.

Among the reporters was Hannah Arendt, a German Jewish philosopher who had fled the Nazis herself.[^scholem] She had been arrested by the Gestapo in 1933, escaped to France, been held in an internment camp there in 1940, escaped again, and reached New York in 1941. Her book *The Origins of Totalitarianism* (1951) had made her famous. She went to Jerusalem for *The New Yorker*, expecting, she said, to see a monster.

What she saw was a middle-aged official who spoke in bureaucratic clichés, corrected small details of dates and departments, and insisted that he had had nothing against Jews personally. He had done his job, he said, and done it well; he had followed orders and the law. "Officialese is my only language", he told the court. According to Arendt, half a dozen psychiatrists had certified him as normal. He even claimed to have lived according to Kant's categorical imperative, from lesson 15, which he took to mean doing your duty as the law commands.

In her book *Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil* (1963), Arendt concluded that the trouble with Eichmann was precisely that so many were like him, "neither perverted nor sadistic" but "terribly and terrifyingly normal". She did not mean that what he had done was banal, or that he was innocent. She meant that great evil did not require a demonic character. It could be carried out by an ambitious, unremarkable man whose main failing was what she called **thoughtlessness**: an inability, or refusal, to think about what he was doing from the standpoint of anyone else, especially his victims.

options.ask: Under enough pressure from authority and the people around them, could most ordinary people be led to take part in great evil?
choices: Yes, most could
Some could, but most would refuse
No: it takes a particular kind of person
Not sure
who: You chose the answer suggested by Arendt and by Milgram's experiments in the next part.
You chose the answer many historians give, who stress that people under the Nazis made real choices and some refused.
You chose the view Arendt wrote against.
The evidence in the next part has been argued over for 60 years.

blocks.text: In July 1961, three months after the trial opened, a psychologist at Yale, Stanley Milgram, began a series of experiments that seemed to bear Arendt out. Volunteers were told they were taking part in a study of learning. Each was told to give electric shocks to a "learner" in the next room whenever he answered wrongly, raising the voltage each time, up to a switch marked 450 volts. The learner was an actor and received no shocks, but the volunteers did not know that. As the voltage rose he cried out, begged to stop, and then fell silent. When volunteers hesitated, a man in a grey lab coat told them calmly to continue.

Before the experiments, psychiatrists Milgram asked predicted that only a tiny fraction would go to the end. In the best-known version, 26 of 40, nearly two thirds, went all the way to 450 volts. Milgram wrote that ordinary people, simply doing their jobs and without any particular hostility, can become agents in a terrible destructive process.[^milgram]

Arendt's book caused an uproar, mostly over a few pages about the Jewish councils that the Nazis forced to help organise deportations, which many readers took as blaming the victims. Her old friend, the scholar Gershom Scholem, wrote to accuse her of having no love for the Jewish people. She replied that she had never loved any people or collective, only persons, and lost many friends.

Later historians raised a different objection. Tapes and notes from interviews Eichmann gave to a Dutch Nazi journalist in Argentina in the 1950s, studied in full only decades later, show a committed antisemite who boasted of his work and said he regretted that not all the Jews had been killed. The philosopher Bettina Stangneth argued in 2011 that the grey bureaucrat in the glass booth was a performance put on to save his life, and that Arendt, who did not know the tapes in full, was taken in.[^tapes]

Even if Eichmann himself was not banal, the idea may still be true of many others, the clerks, railway officials and police who did their part of the work without strong feelings either way. Arendt's own verdict was not softened by it. The book ends with what she thought the judges should have said to him: since he had supported and carried out a policy of not wanting to share the earth with the Jewish people and others, "we find that no one, that is, no member of the human race, can be expected to want to share the earth with you. This is the reason, and the only reason, you must hang."

options.ask: Someone carries out orders to do great harm, without hating anyone, because it is their job. Are they as guilty as the person who gave the orders?
choices: Yes: in politics, obeying is supporting
Guilty, but less than the one who gave the orders
No: the guilt lies with whoever gave the orders
Not sure
who: You chose Arendt's answer: "in politics obedience and support are the same".
You chose the answer most courts give, which treats orders as reducing guilt but not removing it.
You chose Eichmann's defence. The Nuremberg principles of 1950 rejected it.
Many judges have struggled with exactly this question.

blocks.text: The banality of evil is still argued over, by historians, philosophers and psychologists. Most historians now think Eichmann himself was more fanatical than Arendt saw, but the broader claim, that ordinary people in ordinary jobs carried out most of the Holocaust, is supported by later research, such as Christopher Browning's study of a police battalion of middle-aged Hamburg men who shot thousands of Jews in Poland. Milgram's experiments are still discussed, though later re-examination of his records found that many volunteers doubted the shocks were real, and that the lab coat's orders were less scripted than he reported. Arendt's other books, on totalitarianism and on what she called the human condition, are widely read in political philosophy.

blocks.caption: Four questions on Arendt
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What did Arendt mean by the banality of evil?
choices: Great evil can be carried out by unremarkable people through thoughtlessness, not demonic hatred
The crimes of the Holocaust were not very serious
Evil is common and so should not be punished
Only bureaucrats are capable of evil
items.why: She meant that the doer was ordinary, not that the deeds were.

items.ask: What did Arendt mean by Eichmann's thoughtlessness?
choices: His failure to think about what he was doing from the standpoint of others, especially his victims
His lack of intelligence
His inability to remember the details of his work
His refusal to answer the court's questions
items.why: He spoke in clichés and saw his work only as a job well done.

items.ask: What did Milgram's best-known experiment find?
choices: Nearly two thirds of volunteers went to the highest shock when told to continue
Almost no one obeyed once the learner cried out
Volunteers obeyed only when paid more
Most volunteers refused to take part at all
items.why: Psychiatrists had predicted a tiny fraction would go to the end.

items.ask: What did later historians find about Eichmann himself?
choices: Interviews from Argentina show a committed antisemite, suggesting his manner at the trial was partly a performance
He had never worked for the SS
He had tried to save Jews in secret
He was found mentally ill by the court
items.why: Stangneth argued in 2011 that Arendt had been taken in.

summary: **Eichmann was captured in 1960 and tried in Jerusalem in 1961.** He had organised the transports of the Holocaust.
**Arendt expected a monster and found a normal man.** He spoke in clichés and said he had done his job.
**The banality of evil means ordinary doers, not ordinary deeds.** Its root was thoughtlessness.
**Milgram's volunteers mostly obeyed to the end.** Nearly two thirds went to 450 volts.
**Eichmann himself may have been performing.** His interviews in Argentina show a committed antisemite.
**In politics, Arendt said, obedience and support are the same.** Following orders is no defence.

milgram.title: Did Milgram know about Eichmann?
milgram.text: Milgram, the son of Jewish immigrants, said he had the Holocaust in mind from the start, and in his 1974 book Obedience to Authority he quoted Arendt's idea of the banality of evil with approval.

tapes.title: The Sassen interviews
tapes.text: In 1957 Eichmann recorded long conversations with Willem Sassen, a Dutch former SS member in Buenos Aires. Parts reached the prosecution in 1961, but the court admitted only a little of them, and the full material was examined only from the late 1990s.

scholem.title: Heidegger's student
scholem.text: As a student in the 1920s, Arendt had a love affair with her teacher Martin Heidegger, who later joined the Nazi party. She renewed their friendship after the war, which her critics have never forgiven.
